transcript.text: We had a power cut last night and now our Candy washer dryer is completely dead - no lights, nothing. Everything else in the house came back on. The plug fuse is fine, I swapped it. Help!

I am sorry to hear that your appliance has gone silent. Since everything else in the house is working and you have already verified the plug fuse, we need to look at the specific safety mechanisms built into modern washing machines, particularly Candy models.

Here is a step-by-step troubleshooting guide, ordered from most likely to least likely causes:

### 1. Check for an Internal Trip Switch or Reset Button
Many modern Candy washing machines have a thermal cut-out or an internal reset button that trips if there was a sudden power surge or fluctuation during the outage.
• Look behind the machine: Unplug it first. Check the back of the unit near where the cable enters. Some models have a small red or black reset button (often labeled "Reset" or with a symbol like ⏻). Press it firmly.
• Check the control panel: Sometimes, after a power cut, you need to hold down a specific combination of buttons (e.g., Start/Pause + Spin) for 3–5 seconds to reset the electronic board. Consult your manual if possible, but try holding the Start/Pause button for 10 seconds while plugged in.

### 2. Inspect the Power Cable and Socket Connection
Even though the plug fuse is fine, the connection might be loose or damaged.
• Unplug and replug firmly: Ensure it’s fully seated in the wall socket.
• Try a different socket: Plug the washer into another working socket in the house (preferably one that isn’t on a separate ring main) to rule out a faulty outlet.
• Check the cable for damage: Look along the entire length of the power cord for any signs of burning, melting, or chew marks (if you have pets). If the cable feels hot near the plug end, do not use it further.

### 3. Check the Circuit Breaker/Fuse Box
You mentioned "everything else came back on," but sometimes individual circuits can trip independently.
• Go to your fuse box/consumer unit: Look for a switch that is in the middle (tripped) position or turned off. It might be labeled "Kitchen," "Laundry," or "General." Flip it fully off, then back on.
• RCD/RCBO Test: If you have an RCD button (usually orange or blue), press the "Test" button to ensure it’s functioning, but more importantly, check if any RDC trips when you plug in the washer. If it does, there is a short circuit inside the machine.

### 4. Water Inlet Valve Issue (Less Likely for "Dead" State)
If the machine has no power at all, this is unlikely to be the cause of the dead state, but if it powers on later and fails to start, check that water taps are open and hoses aren’t kinked.

### 5. Electronic Control Board Failure (Most Serious)
Power cuts can sometimes send voltage spikes through the mains, damaging sensitive electronic components like the main PCB (Printed Circuit Board).
• Signs: If you’ve tried all above steps and there is still absolutely no response (no lights, no beeps), the control board may have failed.
• Action: This requires professional repair. Do not attempt to open the back panel unless you are qualified, as there are capacitors that can hold a charge.

### Immediate Next Steps:
1.  Unplug the machine for 5–10 minutes. This allows any residual power in the capacitors to drain and may reset the electronics.
2.  Plug it back into a different socket.
3.  Try turning it on. If no lights appear, check for an internal reset button (as mentioned in Step 1).
4.  If still dead, contact Candy Customer Support or a qualified appliance repair technician. Mention that the failure occurred after a power cut, as this helps diagnose potential surge damage.

⚠️ Safety Warning: Do not attempt to open the main casing of the washing machine unless you are a qualified electrician/appliance engineer. There is risk of electric shock even when unplugged due to stored energy in capacitors.

Let me know if any lights appear after the 10-minute unplug rest, and I can guide you further!

I've already tried another socket - a lamp works fine in the one it's plugged into, and I left it unplugged for over 10 minutes, still dead. Consumer unit/RCD are all on and the cable and plug look fine. I can't see any reset button, and I won't take the back panel off. Is it the control board then?

It is certainly possible that the control board has failed, but before we jump to that conclusion, there are two other "silent killers" in Candy washing machines that often mimic a dead control board after a power cut or surge.

Since you’ve ruled out the socket and cable, here are the next most likely culprits:

### 1. The Thermal Cut-Out (Thermal Fuse)
This is a very common failure point after a power surge or if the machine overheated slightly before the cut. It’s a small safety device inside the machine that blows like a fuse to protect the rest of the electronics. If it’s blown, the machine gets zero power, exactly as you’re describing.
• Location: On most Candy models, this is located near where the main power cable enters the back of the machine or sometimes near the heating element at the bottom front. It looks like a small white ceramic or plastic component with two wires attached to it.
• Test: You’ll need a multimeter set to continuity (ohms). If you get no reading (infinite resistance), it’s blown and needs replacing. They are cheap (£5–£10) and relatively easy to swap if you’re comfortable using basic tools, though it does involve removing the top or rear panel depending on the model.

### 2. The Door Lock Mechanism
Candy machines have a safety interlock that prevents operation if the door isn’t securely locked. If this mechanism fails (or gets stuck in an "unlocked" state due to a power glitch), the control board will refuse to power up any lights or functions as a safety precaution.
• Test: Try opening and closing the door firmly several times. Listen for a distinct click. Sometimes, gently wiggling the door while trying to turn it on can help if the lock is slightly misaligned.

### 3. The Control Board Itself
If both the thermal cut-out and door lock are functioning correctly, then yes, the control board (the main PCB) is likely damaged by the power surge or voltage fluctuation during the outage. Modern electronic boards are sensitive to spikes, and a sudden loss of power followed by restoration can sometimes fry capacitors or other components on the board.

### Recommendation:
1. Check the thermal cut-out first. It’s the cheapest and easiest component to verify if you have a multimeter. If it’s blown, replacing it might solve the problem entirely.
2. If the thermal cut-out is fine, then the control board is the most probable cause. At this point, you’d need to decide whether to replace the entire control board (which can be expensive and requires technical skill) or consider if the machine is beyond economical repair, especially if it’s more than 5–7 years old.

Would you like guidance on how to safely access and test the thermal cut-out?

I haven't got a multimeter and I won't open the machine up, so I can't test the thermal cut-out. The door is closed properly though. Is there anything else I can check from the outside, or should I get an engineer in? It may still be under an extended warranty but I'm not sure.

Since you can’t open it up and don’t have a multimeter, we’ve hit the limit of what’s safe to diagnose without tools. However, before calling for an engineer, there are two "outside-only" checks that might save you from an unnecessary visit:

### 1. Check Your Extended Warranty
This is your best first step. Many extended warranties (like those from Currys, John Lewis, or specific appliance insurers) cover "electronic failure due to power surges," which is exactly what a dead board looks like after a cut.
• Look for any paperwork or emails regarding an extended warranty. If you have one, call them first—they might send the part or even replace the whole machine if it’s deemed beyond repair.

### 2. The "Hard Reset" (Power Drain)
Sometimes, residual charge in the capacitors on the control board can cause a "lock-up" where the electronics are frozen.
• Unplug the machine again and leave it for at least 30 minutes (longer is better). This allows any stored electricity to fully dissipate from the internal components.
• After 30 minutes, plug it back in directly into the wall (not a power strip) and try turning it on. If nothing happens at all—no lights, no beep—it strongly suggests an internal hardware failure rather than a software glitch.

### Should you call an engineer?
If the hard reset doesn’t work, yes, you should get an engineer in. Given that:
• The plug and cable are fine.
• The door is locked properly.
• It’s completely dead (no lights at all).
• You’ve already tried multiple sockets.

The most likely cause is either a blown thermal cut-out or a failed control board. Both require opening the machine to replace, which isn't something you should attempt without proper tools and knowledge of electrical safety.

If you’re out of warranty, ask the engineer for a quote on parts vs. replacement cost—sometimes it’s more economical to buy a new machine if the repair involves both labor and expensive electronic components.
